new.title: Compound Interest
sample: This topic was split out of **Simple & Compound Interest** so that compound interest can be learnt on its own. The paper counts and timed drills are in that topic's Quick revision tab; the questions that mix both kinds stay there too.
revision: **One idea:** each period multiplies the money. 10% multiplies by 1.1.
**Two years quick:** rate + rate + (rate x rate) / 100. Different rates: r1 + r2 + r1 x r2 / 100.
**Half-yearly / quarterly:** half or a quarter of the rate; twice or four times the periods.
**Multiples:** they multiply. Doubles in 4 years: 8 times in 12.
**Neighbouring years:** later / earlier = multiplier. Walk back by dividing.
**CI - SI, same sum and rate:** 2 years: r x r / 100 percent. 3 years: 3 r x r / 100 + r x r x r / 10,000 percent.
**Traps.** Interest or amount? "Third year alone" is not three years. Do not halve a compound percent to get a yearly rate.

intro: Compound interest is simple interest with one change: each year's interest is added to the money, so next year's slice is bigger. The habit stays the same: **call the sum 100% and find what 1% is worth.**
There are seven short lessons. The first is taken from the combined Simple & Compound Interest topic; the other six fill the gaps, each with its own practice set. Go in order the first time.
after: That is compound interest. The combined **Simple & Compound Interest** topic now puts both kinds in one question, the way recent papers set them.
Loans repaid in instalments are left out on purpose: they have not appeared in the Clerk papers checked.

lessons.title: What compound interest is
lessons.plain: New: interest that earns interest. Each year's slice is cut from the grown amount, not from the original sum.
teach: In simple interest the yearly slice never changes. **Compound interest** (CI) is different in one way only: at the end of each year the interest is **added to your money**, and next year's slice is cut from that bigger amount.
Take Rs 6,000 at 10% a year.
- Year 1: 10% of 6,000 = 600. You now have 6,600.
The total interest is 600 + 660 = Rs 1,260. Simple interest would have given 600 + 600 = 1,200. The extra Rs 60 is the interest earned on the first year's interest.
Going year by year always works, and you should do it that way until it feels natural. For **two years** there is also a quick route. The interest percent for two years is:
**rate + rate + (rate x rate) / 100**
At 10%: 10 + 10 + 1 = 21%. And 21% of 6,000 is 1,260, the same answer in one step. The first two pieces are the two yearly slices; the last piece is the interest on interest.
If the rate is different in each year, the same idea holds: first rate + second rate + (first x second) / 100.
These two-year percents come up so often that it helps to recognise them. There is no need to memorise the table today; it will stick with practice.
| Rate | CI percent for 2 years |
For three years, do two years first and then one more year on the amount.

example.q: Find the compound interest on Rs 8,000 at 20% per annum for 2 years.
steps: Year 1: 20% of 8,000 = 1,600. The money is now 9,600.
Year 2: 20% of 9,600 = 1,920. The money is now 11,520.
Quick route to confirm: 20 + 20 + (20 x 20) / 100 = 44%, and 44% of 8,000 = 3,520.

check.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 5,000 at 20% per annum for 2 years?
check.why: Year 1: 1,000, giving 6,000. Year 2: 20% of 6,000 = 1,200. Total 2,200. (2,000 is the simple interest; 7,200 is the amount.)

more.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 1,000 at 10% per annum for 3 years?
more.why: Year 1: 100, giving 1,100. Year 2: 110, giving 1,210. Year 3: 121, giving 1,331. Interest = 100 + 110 + 121 = 331. (1,331 is the amount.)

shortcut.title: Rates as fractions
text: Some rates are simple fractions, and then compound interest becomes a ratio. 20% is 1/5: every year, each 5 rupees become 6.
So after one year, sum : amount = 5 : 6. After two years, 25 : 36. After three, 125 : 216.
| Rate | As a fraction | Sum : amount after 2 years |
This is most useful backwards. "A sum amounts to Rs 7,200 in 2 years at 20%": 36 parts = 7,200, so one part is 200 and the sum, 25 parts, is Rs 5,000.

lessons.title: Three years, and a different rate each year
lessons.plain: New: more than two years, and rates that change from year to year.
teach: Compound interest **multiplies** the money each year. 10% a year multiplies by 1.1; 20% by 1.2; 15% by 1.15.
For several years, multiply the multipliers. Three years at 10%: 1.1 x 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.331, so the amount is 133.1% of the sum and the interest is 33.1%.
If the rate changes each year, multiply the different multipliers: 20%, 10%, 25% gives 1.2 x 1.1 x 1.25 = 1.65. The interest is 65% of the sum.
| Rate | 3-year multiplier | Interest |
Fractions are often quicker: 15% = 3/20, so each year 20 becomes 23, and over 3 years 8,000 becomes 12,167. If an answer is an amount like 12,167, look for a cube like 23 x 23 x 23.
"36 months" is just 3 years.

example.q: A sum amounts to Rs 8,640 in 2 years at 20% compound interest. It is then left for one more year at 25%. Find the sum and the final amount.
steps: One more year at 25% multiplies by 1.25: 8,640 x 1.25 = 10,800.
example.answer: The sum is Rs 6,000 and the final amount is Rs 10,800.

check.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 5,000 for 3 years if the rates are 10%, 20% and 10% for the three years?
check.why: 1.1 x 1.2 x 1.1 = 1.452, so the interest is 45.2% of 5,000 = 2,260. (2,000 is simple interest; 7,260 is the amount.)

lessons.title: Half-yearly and quarterly
lessons.plain: New: the interest is added more often than once a year.
teach: When interest is added every half year, each half year is its own period. **Halve the rate and double the number of periods.**
20% a year, compounded half-yearly, for 1 year: 10% twice. Multiplier 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.21, interest 21%.
**Quarterly:** a quarter of the rate, four periods a year. 20% quarterly is 5% per quarter; 9 months is 3 quarters; 15 months is 5 quarters.
| Per year | Compounded | Rate per period | Periods in 1 year | Interest in 1 year |
After that it is the same as yearly compound interest: multiply the period multipliers, or for two periods use rate + rate + (rate x rate) / 100.

example.q: Find the compound interest on Rs 16,000 for 1 year at 10% per annum, compounded half-yearly.
steps: Half the rate: 5% per half year, for 2 half years.

check.q: What is the compound interest on Rs 10,000 for 1 year at 12% per annum, compounded half-yearly?

lessons.title: "It doubles", "8 times", "1.69 times"
lessons.plain: New: compound growth described as a multiple, with no rupees.
teach: Under compound interest the money is **multiplied** by the same number in every equal stretch of time. So multiples combine by multiplying, not adding.
If a sum doubles in 4 years: after 8 years it is 2 x 2 = 4 times, after 12 years 8 times, after 16 years 16 times.
So to answer "when will it be 32 times?", ask **how many doublings make 32**: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2, five doublings.
| It becomes | in T years | Then N times takes |
| 2 times | 4 | 8 times: 3 doublings, 12 years |
| 3 times | 4 | 27 times: 3 triplings, 12 years |
| 8 times | 12 | 2 times every 4 years; 32 times: 20 years |
For **two years**, a multiple that is a perfect square gives the rate at once: 1.69 = 1.3 x 1.3, so the rate is 30%. 1.44 = 1.2 x 1.2, 20%. 1.21, 10%.
Compare simple interest: there, "doubles" means adding 100% each time, so 3 times takes twice as long as 2 times. Do not mix the two up.

example.q: A sum becomes 4 times itself in 6 years at compound interest. In how many years will it become 64 times?

check.q: At what rate of compound interest does a sum become 1.44 times itself in 2 years?
check.why: 1.44 = 1.2 x 1.2, so each year multiplies by 1.2: 20%. (22% halves the 44% growth, which is the simple-interest way.)

lessons.title: From one year to the next
lessons.plain: New: the question gives the amount, or the interest, of two different years.
teach: One more year of compound interest multiplies the money by the same number every time. So **divide one year's figure by the year before** to find the rate.
Amounts Rs 6,292 after 2 years and Rs 6,921.20 after 3 years: 6,921.2 / 6,292 = 1.1, so the rate is 10%.
The same works for **interest of one year alone**: the second year's interest is the first year's interest x 1.1 at 10%.
The interest of one year alone, in terms of the sum:
| Year | Interest of that year alone |
| 1st | rate% of the sum |
| 2nd | rate% of the amount after 1 year |
| 3rd | rate% of the amount after 2 years |
At 20%: the third year's interest is 20% of 1.44 x sum = 28.8% of the sum.
Amounts after 3 and 6 years: their ratio is the 3-year multiplier. 1.728 is 1.2 x 1.2 x 1.2, so 20%.
Once you know the rate, **walk back** to the sum by dividing.

example.q: The compound interest on a sum for the 2nd year alone is Rs 1,320 at 10% per annum. Find the sum.
steps: The 2nd year's interest is 10% of the amount after 1 year.
So the amount after 1 year is 1,320 / 0.1 = 13,200.

check.q: A sum amounts to Rs 7,200 in 2 years and Rs 8,640 in 3 years at compound interest. What is the rate?
check.why: 8,640 / 7,200 = 1.2, so 20%. (Treating 1,440 as a fraction of the sum gives the wrong rate: the year's interest is cut from 7,200, not from the sum.)

lessons.title: Compound against simple: the gap
lessons.plain: New: the same sum and rate under both kinds, and only the gap is given.
teach: For the **same sum, same rate**, compound interest beats simple interest only because of interest on interest.
**2 years:** the gap is (rate x rate) / 100 percent of the sum. At 10%, 1%; at 15%, 2.25%; at 18%, 3.24%.
**3 years:** the gap is 3 x (rate x rate) / 100 + (rate x rate x rate) / 10,000 percent of the sum. At 10%, 3.1%; at 5%, 0.7625%; at 20%, 12.8%.
So every gap question is one division: gap in rupees / gap percent = 1% of the sum.
Backwards: if the sum and the 2-year gap are given, gap / sum x 100 = (rate x rate) / 100, and the rate is the square root.
This lesson is taken from the combined topic, where the gap also appears with two different rates or two different sums.

example.q: The difference between compound and simple interest on a sum for 2 years at 12% per annum is Rs 72. Find the sum.
steps: 2-year gap percent = 12 x 12 / 100 = 1.44% of the sum.

check.q: What is the difference between compound and simple interest on Rs 20,000 for 3 years at 10% per annum?
check.why: 3-year gap at 10% = 3 + 0.1 = 3.1% of 20,000 = 620. (200 is the 2-year gap; 600 forgets the small last piece.)

lessons.title: Two compound schemes
lessons.plain: New: two sums, each under compound interest, compared or added.
teach: As with simple interest, **write each scheme's interest percent first**, then apply it to its own sum.
**Sums in a ratio:** 3 parts at 44% and 4 parts at 32.25% give 3 x 44 + 4 x 32.25 = 261 part-percents. Match to the rupees.

**Equal amounts later:** if two sums at the same rate grow to equal amounts, the one that grows longer must be smaller, by exactly the extra years' multiplier. At 25% for 3 more years, 1.25 x 1.25 x 1.25 = 125/64, so the sums are in the ratio 125 : 64.
**Letters:** x at 12% for 1 year earns 0.12x; (x + 1,000) at 10% for 2 years earns 0.21x + 210. Use the link the question gives.

example.q: A man invests in two schemes in the ratio 2 : 3, at 10% and 20% compound interest for 2 years. The total interest is Rs 3,480. Find the total sum.

check.q: Rs 8,000 at 10% and Rs 6,000 at 20%, both compound interest for 2 years. What is the total interest?
check.why: 21% of 8,000 = 1,680 and 44% of 6,000 = 2,640. Total 4,320. (2,800 is simple interest; 18,320 is the total amount.)
